Now he has brought us singing stones, a shapeshifting piece of origami, and a question about how to speak to people who might exist 100,000 years from now. I’m beginning to see a pattern. What draws me to Lofsöng is the trust it places in the person on the other side of the screen. A shape, a vibration, a patch of light can ask us to stop and work something out for ourselves. I love that. So much of our working life is spent making sure the message lands immediately. Here is a world willing to let us be a little lost. For this next chapter of our , Jesse speaks with Unrelated Studio’s Alessandro Durando about the ideas behind that world, and the people who helped him build it. Put your headphones on for this one. The stones have something to say. On an afternoon at Pier 57, somewhere between the chatter of a dozen playable demos and the steady flow of visitors through the Tribeca Games Gallery, I found myself in front of a screen that refused to speak. No dialogue. No map. No subtitles. Only a small figure in an oversized helmet crossing a gray desert of dust, an origami companion folding itself into the wind, and enormous concrete monuments waiting to be heard. 2026 Tribeca Games official selection , a team based in Turin, Italy. items.page_excerpt: Get the Promonews daily round up Music Video Preservation Society The Promonews mailing list Get the Promonews daily round up Music Video Preservation Society The Promonews mailing list 'Something between a concert, sermon, scam and a possession' Ludovic Gontrand on making Pink Siifu's 'Devil's Advocate' video Paul Nox Bianchi witnessed a jawdropping spectacle on the shoot for US rapper Pink Siifu’s new video, at a Pentecostal church in North London. After its release last month he spoke to Ludovic Gontrand about the creative process behind an extraordinary production. The Ludovic Gontrand-directed video for Devil’s Advocate'! – by Alabama-born hip hop artist Pink Siifu, featuring Ss.Sylver (Siifu’s wife) – opens with shots of a solo cello player and rows of empty seats in a huge auditorium. It's the quiet before a storm that brews over the next minute or so, as through documentary-style imagery, intercut with vintage TV footage, the scene is set for an evangelical religious meeting within this enormous space. Gontrand's video has the sense of capturing a true event. And certainly something special happened on the shoot of the Devil's Advocate'! video. It took place at the Gracepoint theatre in Islington, North London - originally a huge pre-WW2 cinema which has now been renovated as an events space and Pentecostal church - in April this year. Produced by Pulse Films in London and co-produced by Hamlet, who represent the director in France, the video was a passion project, to help Gontrand take the next step following his acclaimed previous videos, particularly for last year. Considerable attention to detail was taken with the casting of nearly a hundred extras for the shoot and also the styling: Siifu and Ss.Sylver's wardrobe includes clothing by cutting edge fashion designers like Yenesai, Luu Dan and La Maskarade. However, Gontrand and the Pulse production team (including producer Katie Scott and production manager Aja Abrahams) were also faced with the problem of shooting the whole video on a short shoot day - the venue had to be vacated before a genuine evangelical meeting took place in the evening. Art Director Flora MacLeod Joins Electric Theatre Collective Art director Flora MacLeod has joined Electric Theatre Collective , bringing a practice that connects tactile CG imagery with an interest in the natural world. She joins the studio’s growing 3D design team, working with Will Denning and James Britton on projects across technology, beauty and fashion. At Optical Arts, MacLeod contributed to Channel 4’s 2023 idents and worked on product animations for Dyson, Aveda and Bowers & Wilkins, collaborating with Fabrice Le Nezet and Dan Tobin Smith. Her project at Outernet London turned the world of plankton into an immersive environment spanning five walls and four storeys. “I have always been really invested in the emotive side of creative work and love when visuals meet sound and story,” MacLeod says. At ETC, she will work within a small design team connected to the studio’s wider VFX and colour departments. Strategy director James Britton describes her arrival as the next chapter for the team, pointing to her tactile approach and sense of aesthetics. items.description: Kendall Goldberg's social anxiety comedy magnifies the fears of every introvert who's ever accepted an invitation to a party with people they don't know.
items.page_excerpt: What’s the Worst That Could Happen? Kendall Goldberg Finds Out in Her Hellish Birthday Party Comedy ‘Surprise’ For many people, heading to any social gathering can be a bit of a nightmare. Especially one where you don’t know the other people who will be there. There’s worry about saying too much, too little, not being liked, not being funny… the list of worst-case scenarios can be as limitless as they are overwhelming. takes that idea and runs with it, when one woman is invited to an intimate birthday gathering and delivers hilarious chaos – as well as a healthy helping of heart palpitations for those similarly hesitant to go to parties. Premiering on our pages today, Goldberg talks to Directors Notes about writing with the film’s star Mary Elizabeth Ellis, collaborating on set with an ensemble cast that includes the great Ray Wise, the challenges of shooting and blocking in a house designed by a mathematician, editing the film herself to find the right rhythm and tone for the story, and working with her composer to create a score that would sneak up on the audience. brings new meaning to asking yourself, “What’s the worst that could happen?”. Where did the idea for this fateful birthday come from and what was the process to bring it to the screen? Mary Elizabeth and I are both fascinated by social anxiety and that feeling when something relatively minor happens and your brain immediately races toward the absolute worst version of how it could unfold. We wanted to take that internal spiral and make it literal. So, I guess you could say we have a shared interest in minor social embarrassment going full-scale catastrophe. Walking in on someone in the bathroom – which I’ve quite possibly discovered is a mild fear of my own – felt like the perfect starting point because it’s so mundane and private, but when you’re trapped at someone else’s house surrounded by people, it can suddenly feel like a cataclysmic pressure cooker. However, most of us will have experienced some moment in childhood when we’re given a glimpse into the adult world. For some, it might be attending a sporting event with a parent, while for others it could be a religious or more symbolic ritual. For the young protagonist, Miguelito, in ), that experience comes in the form of a hunting trip with his father. Of course, hunting carries its own symbolism, and Parra uses this formative experience not only to explore a child’s first exposure to adult life, but also to examine what he describes as the “tension between modernity and tradition, and, above all, the nuances of masculinity”. With its layered themes, impressive ensemble cast and striking production, offers plenty to unpack. So, we invited writer/director Parra to join us on Directors Notes to discuss the personal memories behind the film, his approach to bringing its world to life, and the complexities of the masculinity it explores. Welcome to Directors Notes, Lucas. Before we jump into , I wanted to start by talking about your filmmaking career so far. It’s a compelling format in its own right, operating under a completely different logic than feature films. items.description: Yassmina Karajah unpacks the instinctual performances, voyeuristic visuals and immersive soundscape behind her unconventional love letter to her home city.
items.page_excerpt: A Pop-Up Techno Club Draws Two Lonely Lives into Quiet Orbit in Yassmina Karajah’s Nocturnal Short ‘Ambush’ Set in a dusty, twilight atmosphere, )—which was selected for TIFF, BIFF and SXSW London—unfolds over the course of a single night in downtown Amman, weaving together two parallel narratives that gradually converge. A pop-up techno club takes over the streets, flooding a conservative neighbourhood with heavy bass and unfamiliar faces. On one side, we follow Hasan, who works at a coffee shop and spends his evenings watching the party from his family’s rooftop, nursing an unrequited love and anticipating a long-overdue encounter. Across the street, Jana arrives at the party newly sober, navigating the unfamiliar terrain of connection without alcohol. Inspired by a real night when Karajah found herself watching a group of young men watching the dancers from across the street, is as much about the act of looking as it is about its two leads. It is also a homecoming: her first film shot in Amman, and a love letter to a city she refuses to romanticise. Speaking to DN, the writer/director shares the origins of the project, the creative bounty which results from mixing actors and non-actors, and how a city can shape the plot and characters of a short film. The film began with the image of two buildings facing each other across the street, with people watching and being watched. How did that single image develop into the two parallel perspectives of Hasan and Jana? What was the process of the character building like? came from a real night in Amman right before COVID, when techno pop ups were starting to take place in older, more conservative parts of the city. This club specifically was happening in downtown Amman, which is an area I consider both conservative and touristic, and somehow holds many different parts of Ammani society within it. items.description: A few minutes, a world yet to be fully explored. Helena Ganjalyan and Bartosz Szpak on the deliberate ambiguity and feature-length ambitions of ‘Hauser’.
items.page_excerpt: A Stranger Nobody Can Define Haunts 1960s Rural Poland in Helena Ganjalyan & Bartosz Szpak’s 16mm Enigma ‘Hauser’ A short film, just three minutes long, shot in a haunting black and white style, serves as a starting point for a feature film—or as a mood piece, as described by the directors themselves. Yet, paradoxically, it feels incredibly complete in its own right, despite its very brief running time. That was the impression we had as soon as we laid eyes on . How is it possible that, with barely a hint of a plot and only a sketch of the main character, we find ourselves wanting to understand more, to discover more about the historical context and the social environment in which this story is set? We spoke with writer/director duo Helena Ganjalyan and Bartosz Szpak to explore the deliberate sense of mystery surrounding ‘Hauser’ and, more broadly, the complex relationship between short and feature filmmaking. Their approach also raises questions relevant to filmmakers working within the constraints of the format: how can a brief, self-contained work become the foundation for a feature-length project while retaining the qualities that make it distinctive in its own form? In your version of the story, Hauser is around 47 years old and has spent his entire life working in a small village in southern Poland. The setting of 1964 also moves the character quite far from the historical context in which the real Kaspar Hauser lived. What drew you to this particular time and place? What possibilities did relocating the character to this world open up for you, and what did you want to communicate with this cryptic story? That particular process started actually with architecture. In our original concept for the feature, Hauser lives in a secluded mountain retreat. items.page_excerpt: Fostering The Motion Design Community Since 2006. The Motion Awards 2025 Winners! Dear Upstairs Neighbors: How Connie He Taught a Machine to See the Way She Draws. Pixar alum Connie He on turning insomnia into a six-minute short, tuning a model to her own concept art, and what it took for animators and researchers to speak the same language. Dear Upstairs Neighbors had its world premiere as part of Whoopi’s Wonderful World of Animation at the 2026 Tribeca Festival. Motionographer was in the theater for every short in the program, and this article is part of our series dedicated to the films of this year’s lineup, with more on the way. Dear Upstairs Neighbors. Courtesy of the filmmakers Somewhere in the middle of our conversation, Connie He stopped explaining how she conceived and directed and started marveling at it, as if she were discovering the film for the first time. She was describing the earliest tests she and her team ran on a video model trained on their own concept art. The model picked up a low camera angle nobody had asked for. It picked up the zigzag lines the team drew wherever an object touched the ground, and nobody had told it those lines mattered. “We’re like, oh my god, it’s picking up on all those patterns that we didn’t even think of. That’s kind of an aha moment. We’re like, okay, I think what we are thinking is actually possible.” More than anything else she told me, that moment holds the essence of , the six-minute animated short that previewed at Sundance in January, had its world premiere at the Tribeca Festival in June, and went on to SIGGRAPH in July. The film follows Ada, a woman who cannot sleep because of the noise coming from the apartment above her. The racket summons hallucinations, beautiful and increasingly unhinged, that attack her exhausted mind. Ada, before the night begins. STUDIO STORIES: Tonic DNA, The Studio That Refused to Be One Thing This Studio Story was reported the way most of our lives now happen: on a screen, between New York and Montreal. One long conversation over Zoom at the end of August, recorded, followed by a written questionnaire that Stefanie Bitton answered in her own voice and at her own pace over the weeks that followed. I had cancelled on her twice. When we finally spoke I was running on cold medicine, she was running a studio, and neither of us was willing to cancel a third time. I am glad we did not, because what came through that screen was not a pitch. It was a partner who has spent twenty years inside a studio twice that old, talking about drawings, phone calls, a beaver, a penguin-powered Santa and the people at the desks, with the same steadiness whether the subject was an Oscar or a spreadsheet. What I did not expect was the candor. Twice in that hour she corrected my premise without apology: no, this is a refresh, not a rebrand, and no, 2D never went anywhere, so there is nothing to bring back. When she did not have an answer she said so, and when we reached the film that still makes her cry she let the pause do the talking. A partner with four decades of studio history behind her and nothing to oversell is a rare interview, and it made this piece a pleasure to write. We held the story until Tonic’s new website went live. The refresh is the doorway into this piece, and a doorway needs a house behind it. What follows is not a profile of a studio. It is an argument that a company can change its tools, its model and even its name, and remain unmistakably itself, as long as it protects two things: the people and the standard. It arrives in the month Motionographer turns twenty, about a studio that has been at this for twice as long. I find that comforting. Someone has already walked the road ahead, and they are still walking. This month, Tonic DNA turned on a new website. items.description: Friday Sundae’s Anil Glendinning talks painted memories, ska, singing power tools, and the creative choices behind Tribeca Games Award winner There Are No Ghosts at the Grand.
items.page_excerpt: Fostering The Motion Design Community Since 2006. The Motion Awards 2025 Winners! The Haunted Hotel That Sings Back: Anil Glendinning on There Are No Ghosts at the Grand continues with Jesse Rylander’s conversation with Anil Glendinning, co-founder and creative director of , the studio behind There Are No Ghosts at the Grand. Jesse met Glendinning at Tribeca Games in June and played the game on the gallery floor at Pier 57. What follows is his account. There Are No Ghosts at the Grand, inside the greenhouse. Courtesy of Friday Sundae. Some games tell you their genre in a word. There Are No Ghosts at the Grand needs a whole breath. When I sat down with Anil Glendinning at Tribeca Games, he described it, without blinking, as “a musical, narrative, renovation, horror, comedy, story game.” After spending time with it on the gallery floor at Pier 57, I understood why he didn’t bother trimming the list. Every one of those words is doing work. The setup is simple enough. You play Chris David, an American who inherits a crumbling seaside hotel in England from the British side of a family he has never met. By day, you restore the Grand and the sleepy village around it with a toolkit of increasingly bizarre power tools, some of which talk back. By night, those same tools turn into ghost-hunting gear. There is also a sardonic cat. And, at unpredictable moments, the people of the town break into song. Glendinning is co-founder and creative director of Friday Sundae, a UK studio of just ten people, and he co-directs the game with producer Rachel Glendinning. The game had its world premiere at Tribeca in June 2026 and won the , the festival’s prize for excellence in artistic storytelling, chosen from 12 official selections. Our conversation made it clear that nearly every choice in it, from the textures to the soundtrack, traces back to one idea: a ghost story should feel like a memory. Players at the Tribeca Games gallery, Pier 57, New York. Photo: Jesse Rylander. A ghost story built from a childhood When the team began writing, Glendinning said, they went back to the places that had frightened them as kids. Not haunted mansions, but something more specific and more British.

items.description: Joost Jansen spent two weeks drawing a monster for a film about himself. Then he asked to cut it. Inside DREAMCAT with Joost and MAKE MAMI PROUD.
items.page_excerpt: Fostering The Motion Design Community Since 2006. The Motion Awards 2025 Winners! I’M HAVING A BREAKDOWN: DREAMCAT, the monster that wasn’t his I cannot tell you how DREAMCAT found me. I don’t have social media, and the morning of our call I was still trying to remember who sent it. What I do remember is the behind-the-scenes video. Something clicked, and when something makes me feel something, I pursue it. People need to know what happened to this film after the shoot, when the one they thought they had quietly turned into a different one. That is the story a press release cannot tell, and it is the reason this series exists. When I saw a studio in Düsseldorf and an animator in Brussels spend almost three years on a film combining live action and hand-drawn animation, then throw away two weeks of that drawing because it wasn’t true to the man on screen, I felt something I hadn’t felt in a while. Then I met them, on a Friday night at nine o’clock their time, beers in hand, and I couldn’t believe it either. This is what I’m Having a Breakdown is for. Danny, Joost and Jakob opened the drawers: the plates, the scrapped monster, the Jedi shot that got cut down, the raw drawings and the finished frames. Here is the film they made, and the one they didn’t. The making of DREAMCAT. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen. The monster that wasn’t his Joost Jansen had spent roughly two weeks animating a monster for a film about himself. Then he said it did not belong there. Director Daniel “Danny” Bartels had been bracing for that conversation. Two weeks of drawing were in the cut, and he was still working out how to raise it without hurting his friend. He never had to. After one of the project’s long breaks, it was Joost who came back and said the monster wasn’t working. DREAMCAT began as a portrait of Joost, made by MAKE MAMI PROUD in Düsseldorf, with live action and his own hand-drawn animation. Danny’s first story was a classic hero’s journey. La lumière transforme l’architecture contemporaine en émotion. Découvrez comment elle façonne les espaces, les villes et le quotidien pour les usagers. La lumière ne se contente pas d’éclairer l’architecture contemporaine : elle lui donne du sens, du relief, et suscite des émotions. Naturel ou artificiel, l’éclairage façonne la perception des lieux dans nos vies. Il améliore le confort et valorise les usages. En bref, il rend les architectures vivantes, mais aussi plus durables et plus humaines. [Article mis à jour le : 07/09/2026] Qu’est-ce que l’architecture contemporaine ? L’architecture contemporaine est l’art de concevoir des espaces de vie où la lumière joue un rôle central . Il ne s’agit pas que des sols, des murs et des matières ! Les pour créer des expériences uniques. De la soirée VJing à la battle de prompts. We Are French Touch (BPI) 2025, Scopitone 2025, Stereolux, La Rotonde, MxF Festival… (versions installation et live/VJing) Création, direction artistique & creative technology Installation interactive, Performance VJing, IA Le Carlos Computer Club est une installation d'art génératif et une expérience live A.V. qui transforme le public en co-auteur d'une œuvre en temps réel. Un miroir augmenté capte les silhouettes et les mouvements et réagit aux mots du public (prompts) pour générer une fresque visuelle vivante et sur-mesure. Il se décline en plusieurs formats, de la soirée VJing pilotée par le beat du DJ à la battle de prompts, et a déjà investi We Are French Touch (BPI), Scopitone, le Stereolux et La Rotonde en 2025. Sa signature : une architecture Edge AI 100% locale (StreamDiffusion, 30 FPS, LoRAs sur-mesure), souveraine et brand-safe. Plus d'infos sur carloscomputerclub.com. Éprouvé sur des dizaines d'événements. Calcul 100% local sur machines redondantes, zéro dépendance au cloud. Comme Ars Automata : architecture Edge AI locale, modèles open source, génération embarquée à 30 images/seconde, sans dépendance au cloud. Internet n'est utilisé que dans deux cas : récupérer les prompts du public, qui prompte depuis son smartphone plutôt qu'une station dédiée, ou identifier les morceaux joués via Shazam en mode live. Des LoRAs entraînés sur-mesure cadrent l'esthétique, et le système pilote aussi la lumière (DMX) et génère de l'audio en réaction au public.

Face à quatre grands écrans recto-verso de projection immersive, le visiteur est d'abord scanné pour faire entrer sa carnation dans l'œuvre, puis joue avec les données : chaque point représente une carnation captée par Sephora dans ses boutiques au Canada, donnant à voir d'un seul regard toute la diversité des peaux du pays. Comme creative tech producer, j'ai orchestré la chaîne temps réel (LIDAR SICK, TouchDesigner, moteur Notch, diffusion ETC OnlyView) et le son spatialisé signé Start-Rec. Une œuvre au message fort sur la diversité et l'inclusion. 4 grands écrans recto-verso de projection immersive. Data de carnations captées en boutiques au Canada. Using submission data, desk research, leadership calls, and context from Campaign's journalism, each agency has been studied and evaluated by the editorial team over the last quarter. 2025 was one of the most disruptive years in recent memory for the agency landscape. Omnicom's takeover of Interpublic and the restructures that followed dominated headlines, but other shops were also navigating their own reorganisations. Talent was fighting for a shrinking pool of jobs as mass layoffs and a hiring slowdown became the norm. Bottom third agencies had a challenging year; the reviews reflect the work they need. Thank you to all the agencies that participated despite the time crunch that 2025 was. We hope this is a useful way to distil the key moments of the year and understand the shape of the industry going forward. The Agency Performance Reviews are live for Knowledge subscribers for a full month before moving behind the Information tier on May 17. Further analyses will follow in the months ahead. This year, that changes. The 2026 edition, rechristened the Agency Performance Review, swaps numerical scores and letter grades with a tiered system: Top, Middle, and Bottom third. Here, the Amanita muscaria mushroom pulses and oscillates, unveiling the hidden rhythms of the earth’s soil—a glimpse into the “home of the lives that give us life.” Multichannel Audio and Video Beneath our feet hums another world, expansive and inventive, yet concealed from view. is part of Marshmallow Laser Feast’s Poetics of Soil series illuminating the hidden kingdoms of life underground. This ongoing project reframes our relationship with soil and the diverse species it harbours—from trees and fungi to bacteria, archaea, and protozoa. Each species provides a unique lens on the microcosms that sustain life on Earth, knitting soil into living networks with complexity beyond anthropogenic webs. about presenting this artwork Poetics of Soil: Fly Agaric I at Somerset House, 2025 For at least half a billion years, fungi have played the role of nature’s recycler, breaking down dead plant and animal matter into smaller molecules that are returned to the soil. Circular by nature, this process enriches the soil and makes nutrients available for plants and forest life to reuse. This symbiosis between plants and fungi weaves the Earth’s soils into living networks, comparable in complexity to neural pathways. The relationship between plants and fungi gave rise to the biosphere as we know it. Fungi has long occupied the indigenous imagination, where it entwines with mysticism in science and the interconnectedness of more-than-human species. The Poetics of Soil series seeks to create a window into this unseen world – connecting us anew with these ancient, elemental systems some of us have long been disconnected from.
